title: Two Pointers & Sliding Windows
scopeHtml: Scope: opposite-end pointers, 3Sum with duplicate skipping, in-place slow/fast pointers, fixed and variable sliding windows.

notes.title: Two pointers on a sorted array
notes.html:
Idea. Put one pointer at each end of a sorted array and move them toward each other based on a comparison. Because the data is sorted, each comparison lets you discard a whole group of candidates, so n² pairs become n steps.

Recognise it when: the array is sorted (or you may sort it), you need a pair/triple with a target sum, or you want the best pair of ends (container, palindrome checks, reversing).

Worked example: Container With Most Water. Heights h[i]; the water between lines i and j is min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i). Start at both ends. The shorter wall limits the area, so moving the taller wall can only shrink the width without raising the limit; always move the shorter one.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int maxArea(vector<int>& h) {
    int l = 0, r = (int)h.size() - 1, best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;       // move the shorter wall
    }
    return best;
}
int maxArea(int[] h) {
    int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        best = Math.max(best, Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;       // move the shorter wall
    }
    return best;
}
fun maxArea(h: IntArray): Int {
    var l = 0
    var r = h.size - 1
    var best = 0
    while (l < r) {
        best = maxOf(best, minOf(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l))
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++ else r--         // move the shorter wall
    }
    return best
}
def max_area(h):
    l, r, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
    while l < r:
        best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l))
        if h[l] < h[r]:
            l += 1                            # move the shorter wall
        else:
            r -= 1
    return best

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. The proof idea: when you move the shorter wall you throw away every pair involving it, and none of those could beat the current best.

Everyday analogy. Two people searching a sorted bookshelf from both ends, each stepping inward as they rule out books.

Common interview traps.

  • Using two pointers on an unsorted array without sorting first.
  • Moving the wrong pointer (taller instead of shorter) and losing correctness.
  • Off-by-one: use l < r, not l <= r, when a pair needs two distinct elements.

notes.title: Three Sum and skipping duplicates
notes.html:
Idea. Fix one element, then run two pointers on the rest. Sorting first both enables two pointers and makes duplicates adjacent, so they can be skipped to avoid repeated triples.

Worked example: 3Sum (all unique triples summing to 0).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> threeSum(vector<int>& a) {
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    int n = a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;       // skip duplicate anchor
        int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (s < 0) l++;
            else if (s > 0) r--;
            else {
                out.push_back({a[i], a[l], a[r]});
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;   // skip duplicates
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}
List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] a) {
    Arrays.sort(a);
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    int n = a.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;       // skip duplicate anchor
        int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (s < 0) l++;
            else if (s > 0) r--;
            else {
                out.add(List.of(a[i], a[l], a[r]));
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;   // skip duplicates
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}
fun threeSum(input: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val a = input.sortedArray()
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    for (i in 0 until a.size - 2) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue           // skip duplicate anchor
        var l = i + 1
        var r = a.size - 1
        while (l < r) {
            val s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            when {
                s < 0 -> l++
                s > 0 -> r--
                else -> {
                    out.add(listOf(a[i], a[l], a[r]))
                    while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++    // skip duplicates
                    while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--
                    l++; r--
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return out
}
def three_sum(a):
    a.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 2):
        if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]:
            continue                                   # skip duplicate anchor
        l, r = i + 1, len(a) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if s < 0:
                l += 1
            elif s > 0:
                r -= 1
            else:
                out.append([a[i], a[l], a[r]])
                while l < r and a[l] == a[l + 1]:
                    l += 1                             # skip duplicates
                while l < r and a[r] == a[r - 1]:
                    r -= 1
                l += 1
                r -= 1
    return out

Complexity. Sorting O(n log n) plus O(n²) for the scan, so O(n²) time and O(1) extra space (ignoring output). k-Sum generalises to O(n^(k-1)).

Everyday analogy. Picking a team captain first, then searching for two teammates whose skills add up exactly.

Common interview traps.

  • Producing duplicate triples because duplicates were not skipped (skip both the anchor and the pointers).
  • Using a hash set of triples (works but slower and more memory than skipping).
  • Integer overflow when summing large values (use long).

notes.title: Same-direction pointers and in-place edits
notes.html:
Idea. Use a slow pointer marking where to write and a fast pointer scanning the input. This edits an array in place in one pass with O(1) extra space.

Recognise it when: remove duplicates/elements, move zeros, partition, compress strings, "do it in place".

Worked example: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (return the new length; keep first occurrences).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int removeDuplicates(vector<int>& a) {
    if (a.empty()) return 0;
    int w = 1;                                   // next write position
    for (int r = 1; r < (int)a.size(); r++)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r];
    return w;
}
int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
    if (a.length == 0) return 0;
    int w = 1;                                   // next write position
    for (int r = 1; r < a.length; r++)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r];
    return w;
}
fun removeDuplicates(a: IntArray): Int {
    if (a.isEmpty()) return 0
    var w = 1                                    // next write position
    for (r in 1 until a.size)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r]
    return w
}
def remove_duplicates(a):
    if not a:
        return 0
    w = 1                                        # next write position
    for r in range(1, len(a)):
        if a[r] != a[r - 1]:
            a[w] = a[r]
            w += 1
    return w

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Fast and slow pointers on linked lists are the same idea with different speeds (cycle detection); see the linked-list notes.

Everyday analogy. Packing a suitcase: the fast pointer picks items from the pile, the slow pointer is the next free spot in the suitcase.

Common interview traps.

  • Comparing to a[w-1] versus a[r-1]: both work for sorted input, but be consistent.
  • Forgetting the empty-array case.
  • Writing past the logical length and returning the wrong count.

notes.title: Sliding window: fixed size
notes.html:
Idea. Maintain a window of exactly k elements. Instead of recomputing from scratch, add the new element entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left.

Recognise it when: "every subarray of size k", "maximum average of k elements", moving statistics.

Worked example: Maximum sum of k consecutive elements.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
long long maxSumK(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    long long sum = 0, best;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += a[i];
    best = sum;
    for (int i = k; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        sum += a[i] - a[i - k];                  // add new, drop old
        best = max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
long maxSumK(int[] a, int k) {
    long sum = 0, best;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += a[i];
    best = sum;
    for (int i = k; i < a.length; i++) {
        sum += a[i] - a[i - k];                  // add new, drop old
        best = Math.max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
fun maxSumK(a: IntArray, k: Int): Long {
    var sum = 0L
    for (i in 0 until k) sum += a[i]
    var best = sum
    for (i in k until a.size) {
        sum += a[i] - a[i - k]                   // add new, drop old
        best = maxOf(best, sum)
    }
    return best
}
def max_sum_k(a, k):
    s = sum(a[:k])
    best = s
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[i] - a[i - k]                     # add new, drop old
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n·k) for the naive approach.

Industry examples. Moving averages in monitoring dashboards, "requests in the last N seconds" counters in rate limiters, and rolling hashes (Rabin-Karp) in text search.

Everyday analogy. A train window moving along the landscape: as new scenery enters on one side, old scenery leaves on the other.

Common interview traps.

  • Recomputing the sum for each window (O(n·k)).
  • Not handling k > n.

notes.title: Sliding window: variable size
notes.html:
Idea. Grow the window by moving the right pointer; whenever the window becomes invalid, shrink it from the left until valid again. Each element enters and leaves at most once, so the total work is O(n).

Recognise it when: "longest/shortest substring or subarray satisfying a condition", all values non-negative or a condition that only gets worse as the window grows.

Template.

  1. Expand r, add a[r] to the window state.
  2. While the window violates the rule, remove a[l] and l++.
  3. Update the answer (longest: after fixing; shortest: while valid).

Worked example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Keep the last index of each character; when s[r] was seen inside the window, jump l past that index.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lengthOfLongestSubstring(const string& s) {
    unordered_map<char, int> last;               // char -> last index
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)s.size(); r++) {
        auto it = last.find(s[r]);
        if (it != last.end() && it->second >= l) l = it->second + 1;
        last[s[r]] = r;
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();   // char -> last index
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
        char c = s.charAt(r);
        Integer j = last.get(c);
        if (j != null && j >= l) l = j + 1;
        last.put(c, r);
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
fun lengthOfLongestSubstring(s: String): Int {
    val last = HashMap<Char, Int>()                    // char -> last index
    var l = 0
    var best = 0
    for ((r, c) in s.withIndex()) {
        val j = last[c]
        if (j != null && j >= l) l = j + 1
        last[c] = r
        best = maxOf(best, r - l + 1)
    }
    return best
}
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    last = {}                                          # char -> last index
    l = best = 0
    for r, c in enumerate(s):
        if c in last and last[c] >= l:
            l = last[c] + 1
        last[c] = r
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

Complexity. O(n) time; space O(min(n, alphabet)).

Why it is O(n) despite the inner loop. Both pointers only move forward; each index is visited at most twice. The "while invalid, shrink" form (used for minimum window substring and "at most K distinct") has the same bound.

Everyday analogy. A caterpillar: the head moves forward eating, the tail catches up only when something is wrong.

Common interview traps.

  • Moving l backwards after seeing an old duplicate (check last[c] >= l).
  • Using this pattern when the array has negative numbers and the condition is a sum; it is not monotonic (use prefix sums instead).
  • Off-by-one in the window length r - l + 1.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Two pointers exploit order: from both ends of a sorted array they discard groups of candidates in O(n); 3Sum fixes one element, sorts, and skips duplicates for O(n²). Slow/fast pointers edit arrays in place with O(1) space. Fixed windows slide by adding the new element and removing the old one; variable windows expand on the right and shrink on the left while invalid, giving O(n) because each element enters and leaves once. Remember the monotonicity requirement for variable windows, and use prefix sums when negatives are present.

questions.promptHtml: In Container With Most Water, why does moving the shorter wall inward give the correct answer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the proof behind a greedy pointer move, not just the code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The area is limited by the shorter wall times the width. If I move the taller wall, the width shrinks and the limit cannot rise, so that area cannot improve. Moving the shorter wall is the only move that might find a taller limit, so it is safe to discard every pair involving the shorter wall.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Start with the widest container at both ends. Any narrower container containing the current shorter wall is limited by that same wall and is narrower, so it is no better. Discarding the shorter wall loses nothing. Each step removes one pointer position, so the loop is O(n).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int maxArea(vector<int>& h) {
    int l = 0, r = (int)h.size() - 1, best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;
    }
    return best;
}
int maxArea(int[] h) {
    int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        best = Math.max(best, Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;
    }
    return best;
}
fun maxArea(h: IntArray): Int {
    var l = 0
    var r = h.size - 1
    var best = 0
    while (l < r) {
        best = maxOf(best, minOf(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l))
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++ else r--
    }
    return best
}
def max_area(h):
    l, r, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
    while l < r:
        best = max(best, min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l))
        if h[l] < h[r]:
            l += 1
        else:
            r -= 1
    return best

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Moving the taller wall.
  • Using l <= r, which pairs a wall with itself.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it need sorting? → No; the pointer rule relies on heights, not sorted order.
  2. Trapping Rain Water? → Two pointers with running left-max and right-max, O(n) time, O(1) space.
  3. Equal heights? → Move either one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior gives the exchange argument for why discarded pairs cannot win.

questions.promptHtml: Find all unique triples in an array that sum to zero. How do you avoid duplicate triples without a set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard sort plus two-pointers problem with a duplicate-handling trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Sort the array. For each anchor index i, skip it if it equals the previous anchor, then run two pointers l and r on the rest: move l up if the sum is too small, r down if too large, and on a match record the triple and skip equal values on both pointers. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sorting puts duplicates next to each other, so skipping them at the anchor and at both pointers guarantees each unique triple is emitted once. Using a hash set of tuples also works but costs extra memory and time.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> threeSum(vector<int>& a) {
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    vector<vector<int>> out;
    int n = a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;
        int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (s < 0) l++;
            else if (s > 0) r--;
            else {
                out.push_back({a[i], a[l], a[r]});
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}
List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] a) {
    Arrays.sort(a);
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    int n = a.length;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;
        int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (s < 0) l++;
            else if (s > 0) r--;
            else {
                out.add(List.of(a[i], a[l], a[r]));
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}
fun threeSum(input: IntArray): List<List<Int>> {
    val a = input.sortedArray()
    val out = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    for (i in 0 until a.size - 2) {
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue
        var l = i + 1
        var r = a.size - 1
        while (l < r) {
            val s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            when {
                s < 0 -> l++
                s > 0 -> r--
                else -> {
                    out.add(listOf(a[i], a[l], a[r]))
                    while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++
                    while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--
                    l++; r--
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return out
}
def three_sum(a):
    a.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 2):
        if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]:
            continue
        l, r = i + 1, len(a) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if s < 0:
                l += 1
            elif s > 0:
                r -= 1
            else:
                out.append([a[i], a[l], a[r]])
                while l < r and a[l] == a[l + 1]:
                    l += 1
                while l < r and a[r] == a[r - 1]:
                    r -= 1
                l += 1
                r -= 1
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping duplicates only at the anchor, not at the pointers.
  • Overflow when values are near the int limits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 4Sum? → One more outer loop, O(n³).
  2. 3Sum closest? → Track the smallest absolute difference while moving pointers.
  3. Why not a hash map? → Can do O(n²) but dedup is harder and uses O(n) space.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior generalises to k-Sum and explains the O(n^(k-1)) bound.

questions.promptHtml: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The slow/fast pointer idiom for in-place filtering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use a write pointer w starting at 1 and a read pointer r scanning from 1; whenever a[r] differs from a[r-1], copy it to a[w] and advance w. Return w. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The array prefix a[0..w) always holds the unique values seen so far. Because the input is sorted, duplicates are adjacent so comparing with the previous element is enough. The same pattern solves move zeroes, remove element and partition problems.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int removeDuplicates(vector<int>& a) {
    if (a.empty()) return 0;
    int w = 1;
    for (int r = 1; r < (int)a.size(); r++)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r];
    return w;
}
int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
    if (a.length == 0) return 0;
    int w = 1;
    for (int r = 1; r < a.length; r++)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r];
    return w;
}
fun removeDuplicates(a: IntArray): Int {
    if (a.isEmpty()) return 0
    var w = 1
    for (r in 1 until a.size)
        if (a[r] != a[r - 1]) a[w++] = a[r]
    return w
}
def remove_duplicates(a):
    if not a:
        return 0
    w = 1
    for r in range(1, len(a)):
        if a[r] != a[r - 1]:
            a[w] = a[r]
            w += 1
    return w

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the empty array.
  • Allocating a new array when the problem requires O(1) extra space.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Allow each value at most twice? → Compare with a[w-2].
  2. Move all zeroes to the end keeping order? → Same write pointer, then fill the tail with zeroes.
  3. Unsorted input? → Use a hash set (O(n) space) or sort first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior generalises to "keep at most k copies" with one comparison to a[w-k].

questions.promptHtml: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Why is it O(n) even though the window shrinks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The canonical variable sliding window with a tricky invariant.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Move the right pointer over the string and keep a map from character to last index. If the current character was last seen at an index inside the window, jump the left pointer to one past it. Track the best window length. Each index is visited once by each pointer, so O(n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The check last[c] >= l matters: an old occurrence before the window must not move l backwards. The pointers only move forward, giving at most 2n pointer moves in total.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lengthOfLongestSubstring(const string& s) {
    unordered_map<char, int> last;
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)s.size(); r++) {
        auto it = last.find(s[r]);
        if (it != last.end() && it->second >= l) l = it->second + 1;
        last[s[r]] = r;
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
        char c = s.charAt(r);
        Integer j = last.get(c);
        if (j != null && j >= l) l = j + 1;
        last.put(c, r);
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
fun lengthOfLongestSubstring(s: String): Int {
    val last = HashMap<Char, Int>()
    var l = 0
    var best = 0
    for ((r, c) in s.withIndex()) {
        val j = last[c]
        if (j != null && j >= l) l = j + 1
        last[c] = r
        best = maxOf(best, r - l + 1)
    }
    return best
}
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    last = {}
    l = best = 0
    for r, c in enumerate(s):
        if c in last and last[c] >= l:
            l = last[c] + 1
        last[c] = r
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Moving l backwards when the old occurrence is outside the window.
  • Off-by-one in r - l + 1.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. At most K distinct characters? → Count map, shrink while the number of distinct keys exceeds K.
  2. Minimum window substring? → Expand until all required counts are met, then shrink to the minimum.
  3. Unicode strings? → Index by code point or use a map instead of a fixed array.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains the amortised O(n) bound and the monotonic-validity requirement.

questions.promptHtml: Why does the sliding window technique fail for "shortest subarray with sum at least K" when the array contains negative numbers, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of the monotonicity requirement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A variable window works only if growing the window moves the condition in one direction. With non-negative numbers adding an element never decreases the sum, so shrinking is safe. With negatives, a longer window can have a smaller sum, so you cannot decide when to shrink. Use prefix sums with a monotonic deque (or a sorted structure) instead, O(n).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Compute prefix sums P. We want the shortest j - i with P[j] - P[i] >= K. Keep a deque of candidate start indices with increasing prefix values: pop from the front while P[j] - P[front] >= K (record the length), and pop from the back while P[back] >= P[j] because a later, smaller start is always better.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying a two-pointer window to arrays with negatives.
  • Not discarding dominated prefixes from the back of the deque.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Non-negative only? → Simple variable window with a running sum, O(n).
  2. Count subarrays with sum exactly K and negatives? → Prefix sums plus a hash map.
  3. Complexity of the deque approach? → O(n); each index enters and leaves once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior names the monotonic-deque solution and the dominance argument.

questions.contextHtml: An API must allow at most 100 requests per user in any rolling 60-second period. A teammate implemented a fixed-window counter that resets every minute, but a client found they can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, so 200 requests hit in two seconds and the backend is overloaded.
questions.promptHtml: What is the problem and how would you fix it with sliding-window ideas?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases the limit or adds servers without understanding the boundary burst.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact limit semantics (strict rolling or approximate)? Per-user memory budget? Is this per node or distributed (Redis)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a short burst limiter (for example a per-second cap) while the algorithm is replaced.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The fixed window allows 2x the limit at boundaries; counters reset abruptly; no smoothing.
  4. How I'd verify: Replay a boundary burst in a test and count accepted requests.
  5. Root cause: A fixed window does not look back across the boundary.
  6. Fix: Sliding window log (store timestamps in a deque, evict those older than 60 s, allow if size < 100): exact but O(limit) memory per user. Or sliding window counter: weight the previous window's count by the overlap fraction, O(1) memory with small error. For bursts and smoothing consider a token bucket.
  7. Prevention: Test boundary cases and load test; use Redis sorted sets or Lua scripts for atomic distributed limiting.
  8. Trade-offs: The log is exact but memory-heavy; the counter is cheap and approximate; the token bucket permits controlled bursts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Millions of users? → Sliding window counter with expiring keys, shard by user.
  • Clock skew across nodes? → Use the central store's time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching from fixed windows to a sliding window counter removed the boundary spikes that had been causing a nightly brown-out.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds capacity.
  • Hire: identifies the boundary burst and proposes a sliding window log.
  • Strong hire: compares log, counter and token bucket with memory and accuracy trade-offs and handles distribution.
